utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wonder if I could just briefly raise a procedural matter before we begin. We have a witness, Witness 156, who is scheduled to testify on Thursday. Last week we filed a Rule 70 motion with respect to this witness for -- for certainly Rule 70 conditions, and we also filed a 92 ter motion with respect to this witness. Both could only be filed last week because of the -- we only got the statement a short time ago. In order to have the witness testify on Thursday, we would, of course, need an expedited response from the Defence and a decision from the Trial Chamber on those matters, and I wonder -- we just request that that would be possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can request that of the Chamber, but I'm not -- I'm not aware of this practice where the Chamber makes these requests of the Defence. I don't like it, and I was asked by my staff to do it last week, and I didn't. I think you should find out from them whether they will forgo their right to respond within a particular time. That's a matter between you and the Defence. We will give an expedited response. But let me just ask: Do you know about this? I think your response would be due -- when would their response be due?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't say when the exact date is, but it would be due -- if the 14 days were allowed then it would be obviously sometime next week probably after the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I -- Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe the situation is a little understandable because the Prosecution only got word from the particular government recently. This is a Rule 70 matter, and so they wish to find out whether you would be able to provide a response immediately, I suppose, because the witness is due to testify on -- on Thursday. If you need time to advise yourself, then say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course we don't need any time. A witness from that country had already been here and we are not opposed to having the same situation with regard to this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll -- the Chamber will now -- give its decision later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think counsel addressed the Rule 70 conditions; we also filed a 92 ter motion. I don't know if Defence counsel would be in a position to respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, more is being asked of you, Mr. Tapuskovic. What is your -- you also have to give a reply in relation to the 92 ter motion. I think that reply is formally due on the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm actually focussed on what I'm about to do on during the next few minutes. So could I please be given leave to respond after the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes. All right. We'll get the response later. So let us proceed now with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I'll try to continue from where we broke off last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you first ask you something: In order to deal with that document that I showed you last time, and we didn't manage to deal with it fully, I would like to ask you once again about your statement made on the 26th and 27th of February, 1996. That is D 170, Defence exhibit D170.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, Your Honour, Judge Robinson, could the court deputy please tell me how much time I have left approximately from the time that you've already granted to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have one hour and 12 minutes, and nothing obliges you to use all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope, if need be, you may even add a bit more time to that, if necessary, but I will do my best for it not to be necessary. So could we now please look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, you told me that after the first air bomb that fell on Zuc in January, late January 1994, you spoke to General Arif Pasalic - is that right? - and then you made an offer to elaborate a study on air bombs for the interests of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not a study but it was a survey of the effects of air-fuel bombs. There is a difference involved. And it wasn't for the army. It was just by way of information which was done over a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you spoke to this general and you did that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I saw the effects in January 1994, I thought that it was my duty to inform them of the fact that this was a new type of weapon that had been used in activities aimed against the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement here, somewhere in paragraph 4 on page 2, you say the following. You say that you carried out an investigation in relation to the shelling of Markale 1 on the 5th of February, 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph it says: "I volunteered to investigate the shelling of the Markale market." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I heard that it was improbable to establish where the projectile had come from. I believe that it was possible to determine where the projectile had been fired from on the basis of a proper analysis. So that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is written here is that you stated the following: "When I heard that General Smith of UNPROFOR stated that it was impossible to determine the origin of fire, I decided to contact the Security Service and asked if it was possible for me to conduct an investigation on this event." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They agreed, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went to the actual site, as it says so here, and you introduced yourself to the investigation judge and the investigating judge agreed that you would be the expert?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it's not only that you were an expert then at that point in time, but you were an expert later at the trial of General Galic before this Court?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be sure, Markale I, was that a mortar grenade explosion or was that a modified air bomb? I think I recall it was a mortar attack, but could you please check.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. It was a mortar shell, yes. Markale, the month of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is what it says in the next paragraph, that you stated, that is. "I did not agree with the opinion of General Smith because the Chetniks and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used different shells. The shells produced in Sarajevo were not made of wrought steel, but from pieces of steel or cast steel. By examining the fragments of a shell one can see what kind of steel was used to make the shell." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the translation is not very accurate but that would be it, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you stated on Friday you worked on the manufacture of weapons. Therefore, thanks to your experience from arms manufacturing, on the basis of the quality of the shells, did you make an assessment of your own as to where this shell had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. On the basis of a dynamic analysis of what happened at the target and when the stabilisers were found. That was the reason why I reported. It doesn't have anything to do with my investigation. My investigation was based on something completely different and was presented to this Court here in the Galic case, and in the Slobodan Milosevic case. In both cases, I analysed the situation in detail. Giving indications where the possible firing sites were, and it was established beyond any doubt that the projectile had been fired from a minimum distance of 4.6 kilometres from the actual site. If you look at this here, it is clearly stated what the reasons were why I decided to report and, once I did, there was a clearly defined procedure. My study is here in this court and I presented it several times. If necessary, I can repeat it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, can we say, in view of the fact that you volunteered to do this, that your motives to do so were the same as when you offered your services when the first bomb fell in January 1994? The motives were that you should help the interests of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and your people?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what's "the first bomb"? There is a bomb in 1994, a modified bomb, and then in 1995 when I was appointed by the investigating judge to be a member of the commission. So what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the first bomb that was fired at Zuc on the 29th or the 27th of January, 1994. That is to say, a year and a half before the second bomb.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in my material in my study it says clearly that a student of mine came to pick me up and he asked me to come and have a look at the leftovers of a new piece of equipment that had been used. I came there and I gave my opinion. Let me just inform you of the following. My reporting on the 5th of February, 1994, was an act of reporting to a legal judge. Not to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but to a government organ of the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, a normal state body. So a judge is a legal investigating organ. I reported to him, not to any military organ, and I worked within judicial instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic. But first you were at the centre of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, no, not at -- the centre is the centre of public security, not security services, because an acquaintance of mine was in charge of the Krajlic investigation service there and he was in charge of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know full well what public security is and I know even better what state security is. So tell me what is correct, what is written here or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that is argumentative that -- the way that question is phrased. "I know full well," and so forth. I think that's arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us just attend to the latter part of the question, which is: "Tell me what is correct, what is written here or whatever?" What is the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to the normal police where the head of the crime investigation service who was a colleague who had worked with me until 1993 in the centre for military industry. We were then disbanded, this centre was, and he went there to the crime investigation service to head that service. Since I had his telephone number, I rang him up; that can be checked. It's in that study of mine that was submitted here. This is imprecise. It should be the police, the public security station, whatever the exact wording may be. But that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that you don't understand me.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you excellently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please let me finish my question, and let us bear in mind that I should finish my question so that we do not overlap. So please hear me out and then answer. I have your report on air bombs here and when you spoke about the first air bomb you said that one of your students came to see you and this was in 1994. But here we're talking about Markale on the 5th of February. Over there you do not mention at all any student of yours. As for Markale, you never mentioned that. Could you explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. I did not mention a student for Markale. You got the two mixed up, two different cases. Markale. When I heard on television what it was that had happened and that the official position of UNPROFOR was that it was not possible to identify what was necessary to identify, I called a colleague of mine, not a student, with whom I had worked until June 1993 in the same unit and he had become the head of the crime investigation police in Sarajevo, and I told him then that it was possible to determine precisely where the projectile had been fired from and to assess the possible launch sites and then he called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You never stated that before and I categorically assert that. I'm asking you: Was it the security service or was it the public security?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state clearly that it was the public service police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we're getting to the document that I showed you last time, and it is for the Trial Chamber to see ultimately whether this document can be taken into account as something that should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the witness please be shown D171 now, please, the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see on the document, and we have the version in the B/C/S -- well, not yet, it seems. Last time I showed you the conclusions of the document, and I do not want to read it out yet again. But according to the conclusions the 5th of February Markale explosion was most likely carried out in static conditions. That is one argument. Another argument is that it could not have been fired from the Serb positions for it would have detonated on the roof of the building in that case. I wanted to show you the first sentence in that document whereby you say: "Professor Zecevic handed the team a photocopied report by a Serbian mortar expert scientist, Miroljub Vukasinovic." Is it correct that you had that document in your possession, and is it correct that you handed it over to the investigation team, the people that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence you say: "Professor Zecevic stated that whilst of course the incidents are separate, the information contained within the report is of relevance to the -- February the 5th, 1994, incident." Can you explain what was the significance of that information and how did you assess them?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say here that they were significant for my work. It just says that the report was of relevance for the 5th of February incident. It wasn't important for my study. It concerns the following. My learned friend, Mr. Vukasinovic, in that document analysed an important issue. Once we have a detonation of a projectile, a mortar projectile, it has the casing and the stabilisers, which is rather heavy. The very casing of the mortar round fragments into several thousand small pieces, which have the speed of some 12 or 1300 metres per second or down to 800 in certain areas. The stabiliser cannot be destroyed. It separates from the rest of the body. Depending on whether there is a stabiliser found at the place of impact, if we find it, then the speed with which the projectile hit the ground was approximately the same as at the firing. If the stabiliser was not found, then the round speed was less than at the moment when the stabiliser separates from the body. If the stabiliser buries itself in the ground, we can state that the minimum speed was far greater than the speed of separation of the stabiliser. These are important data based on which it can be determined where the firing occurred approximately. The deeper the stabiliser is in the ground, the distance is greater, the distance where it was launched from. In the case of Markale 1, the projectile was almost 200 millimetres in the ground, which indicated that the place of firing was at least 4.6 kilometres or more, having in the mind the angle of descent registered. As for Markale 2, the stabiliser found was next to the place of incident, which means that the speed, when the stabiliser separated, indicated that the projectile had been fired with a different charge for a mortar round. Based on that, we can conclude as to the distance from which the projectile was launched, and we also knew the angle of descent and it was fairly easy to determine the distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you: Professor Vukasinovic is a well known scientist. He is considered to be someone who knows his math and he used mathematical formulae to reach his conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the theoretical approach he used was very correct; however, some entry data wasn't. And you can see here I'm not saying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, let counsel put his question. What's the question you are putting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, if we look at what you said, that he presented a fair argumentation, are there any grounds in this statement of his, based on your assessment and conclusions, that the explosion of the 28th of August, 1995, was carried out in static conditions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would mike a distinction here. My learned friend, Mr. Vukasinovic, is a good expert, and I have known him for a number of years; however, I cannot discuss his code of ethics, i.e., whether someone would intentionally use wrong data so as to manipulate the result. In the Galic case, I was asked by the Prosecutor to provide my comment concerning several mortar rounds that had previously been studied by Dr. Vukasinovic, Dr. Stamatovic, and another doctor from Belgrade. In the part done by Mr. Vukasinovic, there were many entry pieces of information that were wrong. In the study you mentioned, there are several arguments that are misconceived. If we calculate the height of the building and the distance from the place of incident, we can determine that the angle of descent was at least 70 degrees, whereas in Mr. Vukasinovic's study it says 50 to 60. It changes the whole thing and, I underscore yet again, I want to stress that Mr. Vukasinovic is excellent in theory; however, in his study, he used data that did not reflect the accurate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will soon get to your expert finding. In many cases, you also made presumptions when analysing the incidents. You are never stated things categorically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I address you? When I concluded working on the Galic case, the then Prosecutor, Chester, asked me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The question was that in your findings you made presumptions when analysing incidents. Just answer that for me directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I used presumptions, but I used correct entry data. I didn't try to manipulate as to the height of the building and the distance from the incident. That is what I object to. I do not object to the theoretical mathematical model, but I object to specific things. We know exactly what the height of the building and what the distance was between the place of incident and the building, and you can determine the angle of descent. It is trigonometry. There are no presumptions. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not dwell on this any longer and I know what the OTP's position is. However, I wish to tender a complete translation of this document, since this document was provided by the expert himself, and I would like to have that admitted as a Defence exhibit. It is DD00-2007. It seems that the expert is quite knowledgeable concerning that and he mentioned several details from which I gathered that he studied the document in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object. The witness -- this is a -- this -- the exhibit in question is a paper written by somebody else. The witness has not endorsed the conclusions in the paper or the information in the paper and, therefore, I don't see how it comes into evidence. There's been no endorsement of it. It's a study of Markale 2. It -- I think the only proper way to bring it into evidence is to have the person who wrote it come in and be cross-examined, but not to kind of slip it in the back door this way into evidence when it has not been endorsed by the witness. In fact, it's been -- just the opposite has occurred. The witness has -- has said he cannot endorse it and that it's not reliable. So I don't see how it comes into evidence that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit the document. I dissent in that decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, excuse me. Now that we have accepted your evidence, could you please tell us exactly what it is? Who drafted that report and what is the date of it, and who was it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was drafted by the Military Technical Institute in Belgrade. I don't see any date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1997. They used the data they had and they carried out their mathematical calculations. It is a prominent institute, and I believe this involved the person in charge of the institute. What they used were the mathematical formulae to reach the conclusions they did. In any case, I believe it deserves your attention. As to what weight and importance you will give it, we'll see in the future, once you made your decision on it. I will now turn to the analysis of your findings. I will go to page 62. In English, it is page 68. You recall that I quoted something to you concerning a statement and you said that you couldn't recall anything concerning that. We will go back to that. Under -- or below these photographs it is says the appearance of this modified bomb in the theatre of operations around Sarajevo came after a TV interview with Radovan Karadzic concerning a new secret weapon that would supposedly radically alter the course of the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, but have I a correction to make it. When you asked me the first time I recalled it quite clearly and you are now presenting your own statements rather than mine. It is incorrect that I said that I couldn't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I misquoted you. However, can you tell me when this statement was taken? Before the 19th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you had -- had the information we discussed last time as to the use of -- that weapon being used in other places, in Bosnia, in Krajina, and in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will have to go back to your statement yet again, the statement of the 26th and the 27th of February to ask you about the characteristics of the air bomb. It is D170. In the B/C/S it is page 5. The last sentence of the penultimate paragraph as well as the last paragraph. In the English, it is page 5, the last paragraph. Could you please look at the last sentence of the penultimate paragraph. "About ten metres from the point of impact were large steel containers which showed no traces of fragments, except from a previous 82-millimetre mortar shell." This is what it states. Is that correct? Perhaps we don't have to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you say in the last paragraph: "I went then to the explosion on the road and I saw a crater in the asphalt of two metres diameter and two to 300 millimetres deep. Next to the road was a low concrete wall which was broken and also two houses nearby the explosion and there were no fragment traces on the wall. This confirmed my theory that it was a blast effect weapon and an air-fuel projectile."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should say that it had fuel, that it was a fuel-air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the rest is correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 71 of your report. In English, that is 77. Here you talk about the effects of that air bomb, FAB-250; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you state: "With the use of TNT and aircraft bombs, in addition to the blast effect a powerful fragmentation effect occurs with over 10.000 fragments against objects and personnel within a radius extending tens of metres from the explosion." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "However, with the large number of cases when the FAB-250 aircraft bomb was used in Sarajevo in 1995, the effects of fragments at the scene of the explosion were not strongly evidenced and so a fuel air explosive was probably used." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this is where the misunderstanding was between you and the representative of the security service?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot try to interpret what caused their reaction, but I merely presented my conclusions that they were not interested in the effects. The people investigating were not qualified to discuss that. The very idea of the use of TNT in an air bomb to them meant that it would have a greater effect upon the target, but they didn't want to discuss the characteristics of effects per se. Therefore, I do not agree with you that this was the cause of the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that they insisted upon the idea that the TNT being present presented a great danger for the civilians and the population of Sarajevo. If there was some TNT explosive with 10.000 fragments, which were absent here, their thesis would have been that they -- that they couldn't -- this is what made them conclude that.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure as to how who understand fully this paragraph in the witness's report, because it seems to suggest that one could have both TNT and air fuel in one and the same bomb. Is that possible? Can you please verify this with the witness? Is it -- would it be possible to -- to compose a bomb with both fuel air explosive and TNT so as to get sort of the best or perhaps, rather, the worst of both scenarios?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, that's a good question. That is what I'm moving to, to the pages dealing with that. But the underlying thesis of this entire paper was that there was no TNT, that there was only fuel air material and that in fact this bomb worked through air pressure. If I understand this properly, that is the underlying thesis and the expert opinion involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is only fuel air material, no TNT, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be more specific in terms of your concept. The concept of fuel air bombs means that inside there is a small particle of solid explosive, in this case TNT, so that the fuel air would get out that mixes with the air. Every fuel air bomb contains in it a smaller quantity of explosive, not 90 kilograms like the FAB-250 but, say, ten to 15 kilograms, and the point is that it should break the body, break the casing, and carry out this change, and then secondary fuses act to activate this new mix, and that can clearly be seen on page 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just, for the matter of the record, you were quoted as saying that the FAB-250 would have 90 kilograms of TNT. I think I recall that you said that this would be true for the FAB-100, would it not? So that the FAB-100 would be the one that would carry TNT while the FAB-250 would be the one that carried fuel air explosives, and then only carried as much TNT as was necessary to break the shell, if I understood you correctly. Could you please verify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, the customary usual FAB-250 air bomb, the one that is launched from an aircraft, is filled with TNT. And as such it has 93 kilograms of explosives, of TNT. In this case, that's not what happened. There was less. Just to be break the body -- there was just enough to break the body of the warhead, whereas the FAB-100 has considerably less TNT, 43 kilograms of TNT, and it is used without fuel air explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even what you said now about these minimal quantities is not what is stated in your findings, even if we were to look at the individual incidents involved. But now let us look at page 94. In English, it's 104. The English version moves on to 105 as well. You say here underneath a table: "The FAB-250 aircraft bomb develops an overpressure sufficiently intense to cause the lungs to burst if a person is 30 metres away from the centre of the explosion." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then further on: "The FAB-250 aircraft bomb has over 7.000 fragments with a mass greater than five grammes. An effective individual range greater than 150 metres." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now we're moving on to page 105 in the English version. "This data is the basis for calculating whether an aircraft bomb exploded with solid TNT explosive or a fuel air explosive. If the effect of fragments is not intensive, then this is likely that the aircraft bomb was filled with a fuel air explosive." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First question: In this finding, you did not mention at all that there was a single gram of TNT there.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in the description of the effect it is clearly stated how the system functions, so it should not say here that there were ten or 15 kilograms of TNT. If on the walls, if on the buildings there are no traces of fragments and the body had been destroyed, the destruction has to have been caused by something, and that something is TNT. The actual effect of overpressure in fuel air bombs is that in actual fact it migrates into all open spaces, that the process of the activity or the fuel air bomb lasts 100 times longer than the effect of the overpressure caused by TNT. That means that it kills all the people in the area and destroys all light structures. If you look at the same page that you quoted, if you look at the situation, if the overpressure of 150 kilopascals works in a millionth particle of a second, then there is one hundred per cent lethal effect. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not getting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We -- yes, the interpreters apologise. We thought we were getting from the other booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're talking about fragments found on the walls, possibly in the event that a bomb contains TNT. My question concerns the presence of metal fragments which would be the case if the bombs were handmade, for example by terrorists, or were they special fragments that were due to the presence of TNT?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Of course, there are several types of air bombs. The air bomb that is filled with TNT, when it explodes, the pressure of the explosive and the high temperature of the gas within the body of the bomb destroy the metal body of the bomb. It bursts into millions of pieces and their velocity is very high. But at the same time there is overpressure too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, distinguished witness, after this there are just a few photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of individual incidents as well but this is your conclusion. This is your conclusion, these are your findings, and you do not mention a single gramme of TNT. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very simple matter. When you come to the site, the scene, where a modified air bomb had exploded and when you see that a house had been destroyed or several houses, or if the projectile hit a sky-scraper then you will see that three storey were destroyed. You walk in and see that there are very few fragments on the walls. And that is the objective of my analysis, to say since there is a great deal of data about the activity of bombs with fragments. That is to say, if on walls there are many fragments, if surrounding buildings are damaged, then this leads to the inevitable conclusion that the bomb had solid explosive. If there are no fragments and there is a great deal of destruction involved, there are remnants of the rocket motor and of the body, then what is the inevitable conclusion is that instead of TNT there was fuel air explosive in the body. This TNT which is used in fuel air bombs has only one function, to destroy the body of the bomb and to have it -- the fuel air migrate into the surrounding atmosphere, for it to mix with oxygen and in all surrounding areas. So there is no need for me to mention this specifically. My conclusion clearly says this data is a basis for the assessment whether this was an air bomb with a solid or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. When you talk about the FAB-250 and pressure you say that then there is such intensity that lungs burst for all persons that are up to 30 metres away from where the bomb fell. That is to say, that a large number of people would have been killed, right, within that area?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One per cent. Can't you see that? It says -- I mean, if a person's lungs burst he or she won't get killed. He or she will have a breathing problem. Please look at the table above.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there's no need for me to look at the table. Let me ask you the following: Did you have a single medical document showing that somebody had lost their lives because their lungs had burst?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On television, at least according to my information, there was a man who was relatively nearby, near the site of the explosion, and he had these characteristic effects due to the bursting of his lungs, but I'm not an expert in this field and I don't want to go into that. I'm just telling you what the definitions are and this table only refers to people, whereas in the first part we only speak of buildings, how high the overpressure should be in order to have a building destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But even more importantly, I'm not going to use the fragment, the word fragment anymore, but I'm going to use another word for fragment, "geller" [phoen]. It should act within a diameter of 150 metres if it is TNT, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we didn't hear the word, the other word which apparently is a synonym for fragment. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Geller" in the sense of shrapnel, a metal particle, a bomb is broke down into five-gramme particles. At one place he even speaks of 11.000 fragments or shrapnel that can cause lethal effects or very serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's apparently shrapnel. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since, according to your own findings here, and I don't know if I'll have the time to analyse a few more incidents. In some places there is no reference to shrapnel. In some places there is very little shrapnel. And if I may say so, in some places there aren't any casualties. Is it possible for there not to be any classical injuries such as the bursting of lungs? Is it possible that it was just an ordinary explosion that was supposed to look as if an air bomb had exploded, especially where there were no casualties involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- that the -- I don't know what -- maybe we could have some precision about what the -- what the question pertains to. Is he just talking about any explosion? Is he talking about a particular explosion? I -- I'm not clear on what -- I think the question is extraordinarily vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're asking whether it is possible that it was just an ordinary explosion that was supposed to look as if an air bomb had exploded. Is this in reference to a particular explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially for the explosions where there were no casualties, in view of the fact that within a diameter of 150 metres a lot of people would have had to get killed and within 30 metres a lot of people would have had to have injuries, such as bursting -- lung bursting. I mean, I have to say that one casualty is one casualty too many, so that is my reading of this. But I'm just saying, suggesting that in most cases these explosions were just supposed to look like explosions caused by air bombs, because there are no witnesses who would testify that an air bomb actually fell there. Could the witness just tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting then that the explosion did not take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was an explosion but the explosion was not caused by air bombs. Precisely in view of that, I'm not going to analyse individual incidents now. I'm not going to go from one incident to another because this should be done in the Defence case, and I will do that. But if we were to count the casualties due to these bombs, and please don't take my word at face value counting, but we should look at the effects. The shrapnel, 150 metres, and indeed this is dangerous. However both effects were simply not there, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have evidence of parts of an air bomb being embedded in the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it still doesn't prove anything. In the sense presented here that these were -- these devices which appeared out of the blue, that there were -- very lethal killing everything in the diameter of 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you're asking the witness is this: There was an explosion, Witness, but might the explosion not have been caused by an air bomb? And I understand counsel to be alluding specifically to instances in which he said there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may be that I did not grasp correctly the substance of counsel's question, so I'm going to ask him to put it again. Put the question to the witness, and as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I don't know whether I will be able to put all of your analysis to you here, but at least in three incidents analysed there were no casualties. Having in mind that, that there were no casualties in certain incidents, and having in mind that the overpressure blast effects are as stipulated, as opposed to the TNT effects, is it possible that one can cause an explosion by some other means other than an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell you this. Concerning the overpressure effects and the shrapnel effects, those refer to the solid explosive; it is clearly stated in my study. For me to be able to reply -- well, Your Honour, I cannot reply unless I know whether the explosive was in a casing or not. What was the type of explosive, what primer was used. Therefore I cannot provide the answer the Defence attorney wants me to. If he specifics the parameters, I can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You need some other postulates to support the question and the witness is saying one of them is whether the explosive that you had in mind, or that have you in mind, was in the casing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, my question refers to any type of explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already put to you some documents showing that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had explosives. I'm not trying to say that it wasn't either the fuel air explosive or the TNT. It could have been anything else, any other material which causes destruction on solid objects and does not cause any injures and results in no casualties.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot reply to your question because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can reply to any question which has technical sense. This one doesn't, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you this: There is a solid explosive in TNT in bags. It's not pressed. Since the characteristics of the explosive depend on the type of processing, the effects of such an explosive is important for the initiation points. It is also important whether it is -- the explosive was buried in the ground or simply put on the floor of a house. Therefore, there are a lot of factors for me to hypothesise and to be able to tell you, you will have this or that effect. In any case I studied, we always found pieces of the rocket motor. There was also the penetration into a wall. A solid explosive in a bag cannot penetrate a building. It cannot have rocket motors. That's why this question strikes me as irrational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have heard he is not in a position to answer the question in the absence of your providing further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this can be some additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is Sefer Halilovic's book, The Cunning Strategy. In that book he states that his wife, together with her brother in uniform, was killed on the terrace of their house in July 1993, and that they were killed by a projectile which was guided. He said that he knew the people who were to be blamed for that, and that this was a terrorist organisation. Do you know of that incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of it, but it's got nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my view too. I don't understand the question. Let's have another question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The same way could have been used -- the same mode could have been used in this case, to have it detonated remote, and then we have both the remaining pieces of the bomb as well as the effects which, however, were not dangerous for the population because the bomb contained neither the shrapnel nor the substance that would cause the overpressure. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because if you look at the high-rise or at the impact on the top of the building of Safeta Hadzica, we see the rocket motor, we see that one level was -- that the bomb went through one level, that three floors were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How come you have a rocket motor on the roof of a building, however no casualties?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. People were injured, one killed, as well as a lot of fear due to the explosion. Apartments were destroyed. Well, that's not a casualty, but still. I wish you were present during an explosion of a mortar round near to you, let alone being close to a hundred and -- kilo bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is perhaps a bit belated but it's still relevant. Unless I'm mistaken I believe that all of our air bomb incidents have casualties. So I think it's a -- misstating the evidence to say that there were incidents that contain no casualties. I could be wrong, but I don't think -- I don't think I am in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what incidents are you referring to in respect of which there were no casualties arising from an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think I'll have time to go through it all, but when you read it, you'll see that at least two incidents, according to expert findings, had no casualties. Not a single one. There were several incidents without casualties, even as the witness put it. But in his analysis, I can show you at least two incidents without a single casualty, a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would expect that -- you to have that information at the tip of your fingers, because it's the basis on which you have put the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have enough time. I will be able to show you if you give me another 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I think it's an important issue as to the evidence in this case, so I'm going to take the adjournment now, and when we return, you are to provide me with the information, and I expect the Prosecutor to do the same. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have the information on the matter that I spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've skimmed through it and I found information on four incidents. First and foremost, you asked me to provide an example with no casualties. It is page 135 in the B/C/S, and, in the English, 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 135 in the B/C/S and 150 in -- in the English. It is the incident of the 1st of July, 1995, no casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1st of July, 1995. Is that in the -- we'd find that in the indictment, would we?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the expert finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Unscheduled?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this pertains to scheduled -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me just hear Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This pertains to scheduled incident 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There are -- in that incident, there are casualties, injuries, alleged, and that is clear at page -- if counsel just went a little further, where there is further discussion about this incident, page 154 of the English report, which is, in B/C/S, 138. So this -- this -- this incident does have injuries and we have led evidence on injuries. Either we have or we will, but -- there is no air bomb incident that -- where there are no injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Does that go for scheduled as well as unscheduled incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. That is for all of the scheduled -- that is for all this -- and just to be even more clear, all the scheduled incidents that we are proceeding on -- I believe that there were -- there perhaps were scheduled incidents that we dropped at the beginning of the case where there may -- maybe were no injuries, but all the scheduled incidents that we're proceeding on, all of the ones that were analysed in this report, we allege in the indictment and in our evidence had casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, in the indictment for the incident of the 1st of July, it is alleged that 13 people were injured. That one doesn't appear to support your proposition, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no casualties on the 26th of May, and I've been going through this report for a few days now. In this report, on this given page, it -- it's where I found it. I'm still dealing with the issue with the proposition I put to the witness concerning this, situations where those explosive devices may have been planted. That is the essence, the gist of my line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now are you talking about an incident that took place on the 26th of May? Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I am still talking about the 1st of July, 1995. I wasn't in a position to get all the information about all the specific situations where there were no injuries, but according to the initial indictment there were at least four incidents with no casualty, with explosions only. But could you please direct your attention to the three incidents of the 16th of June. Three incidents in the same day. There were some light injuries and, in the incident of the 16th of July, at page 132 in the English, there are no shrapnel traces, according to the expert report. So three days into the offensive. Let us have a look at those three incidents of the 16th of June. It is page 139, no fragmentation -- fragment traces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask the expert to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you come to the 16th of June, let's go back to the 1st of July and clarify this once and for all. The indictment alleges 13 people were injured. Mr. Whiting, has evidence been led on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not, Your Honour. No, Your Honour. No evidence was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not yet or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that some evidence is coming in this week on this -- on this incident from an investigator. I believe that we may have some victim evidence, but, in any event, it's -- it is not the Prosecution's position in the indictment, in the expert report, or in our evidence that there were no injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, no, let me -- let me speak. In relation to this incident of the 1st of July, the indictment alleges 13 people were injured. Evidence has not yet been led on it. But that doesn't entitle you to say that there were no injuries because evidence has not yet been led.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, I have studied the material. There were injuries resulting from other material, but it was because of burst glass, debris, but not the bombs themselves, and we haven't heard any of it here still. When we analyse this report, we cannot go back to telling the Bench that no evidence was led as to that. Perhaps Mr. Whiting can confirm that those injuries were from shards of glass and other material, like debris, in the -- in the -- not of the shrapnel. In the incident of the 16th of June, there are no marks on the walls --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would have caused the shards and the glass and the debris? Is it not the bomb, the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if it was a planted explosion, if there are no fragments -- for example, at page 132 in the English, there are no fragments on the incident of the 16th of June one day into the offensive. There is not a single fragment in or on the objects around the place of impact. How is it possible? Just look at that page and the expert can tell me perhaps how is it possible that he hasn't found a single fragment concerning this incident of the 16th of June - page 132 in the English and 118 in the B/C/S - not on the walls or anywhere. If it was an air bomb containing 11.000 pieces of shrapnel killing everything within 150 metres in -- with its -- within its place of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the -- it doesn't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think precision matters here, and it does not say that there wasn't a single fragment on the objects or the place of impact. If you look at page 133 of the English it says there are no signs of fragmentation effects in the area around the place of the explosion. I think the witness both in his direct examination, in his report, and in cross has explained, and he can explain again, why there wouldn't -- why -- what -- how he explains that, what his explanation is for the fact that there were no signs of fragment from his analysis. I'm not saying there wasn't any fragments. I'm saying from his review there were no signs of fragments. That is, he didn't see any fragment signs. But he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The report also says on page 132, Mr. Tapuskovic, in English: "Parts of the motors and support structures were found in the crater."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have it all here, but it's difficult to find my way around with so little time. 118, right. The page is 118. I'm sorry, 118. 118. I am sorry, 118. 118. There. The English reference is 134. On the side walls of sky-scraper there are no shrapnel marks. 119, just before that one. This is 120 in B/C/S, and 134 in the English. And the previous page, 119, no shrapnel marks around the explosion site. Two distinct references, 119 and 120, and the B/C/S is 134. 134 for B/C/S, or, rather, for English, and 134 for the English or, rather, the B/C/S is 119 and 120. There are no shrapnel marks anywhere in the area or on the walls for that matter. This is stated quite categorically. Now, how is that possible if there was a bomb that actually exploded there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm confident that the witness can explain that, and perhaps we should go back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you heard counsel's assertion that in relation to this incident the report says there are no shrapnel marks anywhere in the area or on the walls for that matter, and the question is: How is that possible if there was a bomb that actually exploded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a feature of the aerosol generator air bombs, fuel-air bombs, is that they have the -- a wave effect their secondary effects is a fragmentation effect, and that's what I've been trying to prove along. This is the whole point of this report. The point of this report is to show in relation to all cases when an explosion occurred that there were no obvious shrapnel marks, but instead there were effects of destruction. In this particular incident dated the 16th of June, you have the photographs and they clearly show that the bomb penetrated into the ground and exploded once it was embedded inside the ground, and there was secondary fragments, secondary shrapnel which was absorbed by the ground. All that was found were bits and pieces of the rocket engine. So my theory is that no solid explosive was used in this incident, which has a significant fragmentation effect, and quite considerable blast effect but the range remaining small though. My theory instead is that this is an air-fuel bomb, fuel-air effect. This is a very dominant weapon, and you can see that in all of these incidents, and the fragmentation effect with the shrapnel being sprayed all over the place is entirely secondary, which is perfectly consistent with the evidence presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Am I right then in saying that your explanation is that this was an air-fuel bomb and not a solid explosive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, Witness, what you are saying is that when we're talking about modified air bombs, it is possible that bombs may be made with, as their content merely fuel and air, on the one hand, and that there are other bombs which contain a lot of TNT, and that the first bombs may use maybe 15 kilos of TNT simply as a primer, but that for such modified air bombs, it will -- there will not necessarily be a lot of shrapnel, not necessarily a lot of fragments. That's what you're saying? Because earlier counsel for the Defence said, and he quoted a number of incidents in which he was wondering, if I understood him right, whether since there were no fragments, not enough shrapnel, and since there were not enough traces, then maybe they weren't modified air bombs at all. But what you're say something that, in fact, even without fragments, even without shrapnel, it is quite possible that this is a modified air bomb, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is indisputable that this was an air bomb, a fuel-air bomb, and it was driven by a motor engine and filled with an explosive. There are SFOR photographs taken after the war and these photographs are attached to this report. There is no dispute about this. There are photographs of Russian missiles that were also found in Bosnia-Herzegovina by SFOR and not by either of the warring parties, and those too are attached to the present report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tapuskovic, now you have given us two incidents in respect of the basic issue as to whether there were casualties, the 1st of July and the 16th of June. What is the other one, or the others, in which you allege there were no casualties?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would need to go back to the statement that I showed. Before his help was ever enlisted as an expert witness, he listed a couple of incidents where there was no shrapnel and no casualties. I do have to remain adamant about this though. The 16th of June, that particular incident, three missiles, alleged missiles, air bombs. On the 16th of June. We have three missiles on that day, that were subjected to analysis by Mr. Zecevic. With the exception of slight injuries there wasn't a single casualty. These incidents are described in his report. This is the 16th of June, three separate incidents. Except for slight injuries, there wasn't a single casualty. This was one day into the offensive. How can he possibly explain this? Three bombs exploded and not a single death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- counsel is obviously making reference to scheduled incidents 11, 12, 13. In all cases injuries are alleged, and in all cases evidence to that effect has been led. We're now hearing a distinction between light injuries and injuries, but that wasn't the premise of the question earlier. The premise of the question was no casualties. These all -- that -- that there were casualties in all instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because for schedule -- scheduled incident number 11, it's alleged three persons were slightly injured. Mr. Tapuskovic, for number 12, it's alleged seven persons were injured, and in shelling incident 13, W -- witness W-104 and her daughter, who was in the apartment as well, were both badly and permanently injured. And evidence has been led in relation to these.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have examined this matter sufficiently. You are to proceed with the question but not on the basis that there were no casualties, because have you not been able to substantiate that from either the indictment or the evidence to our satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure how much time remains for me to bring up a couple of more incidents to ask the witness about. How much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many more incidents do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like at least two or three. No more than that, because all the other ones are pretty much similar, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. You have another 12 minutes left and let us see how far you get in 12 minutes. If you need more time, then we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's one thing I need to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no incident where you took into account the medical files, was there? A while ago you confirmed to me about the lungs bursting. You never looked at any medical files in order to cross reference those injuries with the possibility of injury, not merely by shrapnel but also by bits and pieces of building material which was a distinct possibility. You never cross referenced that, did you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did look into that but I'm no expert in defining injuries. I am an expert in determining how injuries come about. I'm a designer of ammunition. My job is to create a weapon that will cause an injury. It's not for me to assess the injury itself. This is the job of a medical expert and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, there was no medical expert for you to cross-reference and to compare to your own findings, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the material submitted to me, there were medical findings and submissions by physicians. However, it was my belief that I myself was not qualified to give an opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let me try to tackle what I really believe is necessary. Let's look at the 28th of June, 1995, the incident that occurred on that day. This was when the TV building was hit; that's the incident that I'm talking about. If I'm not mistaken, and I must say this again, before you were appointed as an expert, even then on the 28th, even ten days before then, you observed the effects of those air bombs in an entirely unofficial capacity, as you have confirmed, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you possibly consider to be an official capacity?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not necessarily the issue. But on the 28th you were given the job, and by this time you had already formed a deep conviction to which you stuck throughout the rest of your work, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I always do is I approach the site of an explosion, the scene of a crime. I photograph it, I record the marks, I record the prevailing conditions, and that's what my report is based on. I would be a very lousy expert indeed if I were to define the results of my own work ahead of time or before I take the actual findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 125, B/C/S. The English reference is 140. But before that -- my apologies. I do have to ask you several questions about some general features in relation to the flight of missiles, of bombs, while they're still in the air, I mean. You address that in paragraph 18, 19, 20, and 21, those paragraphs. There the English page is 167 and the B/C/S is 148. Here you say that: "The velocity of a missile is relatively low." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "relatively low"? I was talking about FAB-100, the velocity was 200 plus/minus per second, and the FAB-220, depending on the angle at which it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then number 18, I'm talking about page 167. It has a large mass and it's -- it's easy to observe in flight. It is very difficult -- it is very easy to spot and to monitor.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your reference for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 148.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, a missile can be observed, if you observe its motion laterally from one of the sides. So this is how a missile flies and whoever is observing it is at a certain distance. If it makes a sound, then it's -- it's possible to observe it. However, if a missile is flying towards the observer it is impossible to visually observe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: More about paragraph 19, page 152. That is the B/C/S reference, 171 in the English text where you say: "Given that the launching pads were within urban communities or near forested ground, probably only a small part of the population was near the places that the missiles were fired from and probably very few observed the fact that the missiles were fired."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's perfectly commonplace. If you look at image 128, figure 128, you can see that. The acoustic spectrum is a function of time of an artillery launch. These are an -- American images, and it wasn't until ten years ago that devices were built to detect missiles by way of using an acoustic spectrum in order to more accurately locate a missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the pages that are in relation to the incident itself. 125 in B/C/S and the English is 140, or rather, 141, if you turn the page. So 126 and 141. You established here that it was the investigators' opinion that the incoming direction of the missile was from the general area of Dogladi?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just copied what they had stated in their own report, and then I provide my own comment further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're about to look at that. But let's please first go to the next page, 127, and the English is 143. This is what you state here. You talk about witness statements what various witnesses said. For example, Rijalda Musaefendic heard a sound. Mehmed Kember heard a loud blow. Fadila Serdarevic heard a loud thud. Witness Muhamed heard the falling of concrete and glass, and then they heard a detonation, they heard the projectile fly, and what do you say in relation to Igor Mocnaj? He was outside the building. He heard the missile being fired. And then he goes on to explain what exactly he heard, but he heard the actual missile being fired. And then two paragraphs down you go on to say this: "Two military observers saw the launching and the flight of the projectile low velocity -- low altitude impacting into the north side of the building, the explosion taking place several seconds after the impact." My question: Given the fact that witness Igor Mocnaj heard the missile being fired, does that not clearly show that the bomb or the missile was fired from a nearby position within the area of responsibility of the BH army, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why? We discussed about the features of sound. I said this and you quoted it. If the place that the missile was launched from was in a forested area, or if it was in a settled, built-up area, if you look at the launching direction that I spoke about in my analysis, you will see that there is a flat piece of land there with no settled or built-up areas. It's perfectly flat. You could hear the rocket engines humming, as I said, for about two seconds at least, and then up until 400 metres from the place where the missile was launched from. So as far as the TV building was concerned, yes, you could hear that. You could hear this, you could hear that, but everything depends on specific conditions and each of the incidents were unique. During the testing, I could hear rocket missiles being fired at a distance of between 10 and 12 kilometres, but that is over flat ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have to interrupt you. You say that each incident is unique. This is the only witness who actually heard a missile being fired, not a missile flying. Does that mean that he was near the place that the missile was fired from, which would seem to imply that it was fired from a position under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have just explained it to you, haven't I? This is about the lie of the land; that's what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you even try to assess what the two military observers noticed? Or did you simply not take that into account at all?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did provide a comment right here, didn't I? It's -- it's their comment, actually. Low velocity. Low velocity, about 200 metres per second. It might be low to you, might not be low to me. I told you about those that have the speed of 1.000 metres per second. For me, this is a low velocity and low altitude. An average missile can fly at 400 or 500 metres' altitude. 4.000 to 5.000 metres' altitude, and this one flew at 600 or 700 metre, so that is a low altitude for me, for my standards. You need to define high and low.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was located at 5.800 metres that it flew in from the Butile. Could it possibly have had -- have followed that sort of trajectory, given the hills that would have been in the way?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the photograph on page 131, you can see very clearly that there is not a single hill in that area, not a single forest. This is flat ground unsettled. This is what we normally refer to as the Sarajevo field. This area was farmed. There are no obstacles there, nothing in way of the sound, nothing to muffle the sound of a missile flying through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry that I won't have sufficient time to -- to take you back to each of the incidents, but can you please explain this to the Chamber. Can you explain why you established something that was totally different from what the investigators had established. They mentioned the Dogladi area from the area where the missile was fired and you talked about general Butile area. Is it not because you were looking for an appropriate trajectory for the missile to follow precisely because there no hills in that area?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you. Go to page 126, the upper-left image on page. One can see clearly on the roof of the TV building clear, severe damage, caused by an impact of a bomb against the roof. If you use standard American norms to establish the direction of impact, in the case of a ricochet, and you can see that here, you can determine the direction. You can see the marks that the bomb left on the roof and based on that, I determined the direction, its angle of descent. I defined that. Last Friday I said that the angle of descent was about 25 per cent causing -- 25 degree, causing severe damage to the roof of the TV building. It was also possible to establish the minimum range followed by that particular missile, not the maximum range, the minimum range, and this tallies fully with the result of my own analysis, which itself is very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber why there is this striking discrepancy between the two, the place that it was fired from, Butile and Dogladi. These are two different locations, right, especially in terms of distance, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only explain what I did myself. If you have any other questions about that, I think I can tell you as to who -- why the investigators wrote this or wrote that. Now, this is really not something that I can be expected to comment on, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You took all of those photographs last year, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All these photographs, all these lines that you drew as potential trajectories, you did that in your own office, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please be more specific? Which photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope we're not overlapping, are we? The photographs in your report.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All of them, the whole works. All of the photographs in this expert report that are in relation to these incidents.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I remind you of this: Go back to page 126. Below the photograph in the upper-left corner it says, "photograph from the following document 0032392143." This is a document that I received from the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor obtained this document from the investigators. There are all these photographs.
