They're all clear, and they all say exactly where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please just go to page 1 hundred. It's impossible for me to deal with everything, isn't it? Page 100, which addresses the incident that occurred on the 7th of April. I'm about to provide the English reference. English reference is 112, page 112. Allegedly there is a witness to this incident. That's what it says. The witness who followed the launching of this modified air bomb from the water protection area at the spring of the Bosna River near the village of Dolac. Who is this witness?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is in one of the OTP documents. I didn't care about that witness's name it didn't matter to me. But in documents that I was given there was a witness who watched a missile being launched from Igman and he used his own binoculars to follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is in on o the OTP document and the person's name is right there. Can you please explain how it is possible given the number of incidents that there is no other eye-witness, not a single other eye-witness throughout that summer with the exception of this one?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why I should be expected to explain that to you, why things happened the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, doesn't that show that many never flew at all, they were on the ground before the explosion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. There is absolutely no physical meaning or possible sense to you're saying. Will someone actually spot a missile over a 24-hour period at a location that is an area covering ten kilometres at a given point in time. It's like looking for a needle in a haystack. You need to know exactly where a missile was launched from in order to be able to assess the probability of someone actually seeing the missile fired and following the missile on its flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, just to clarify, your case is that these bombs were actually planted by the -- by ABiH, by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one thing that I can say with certainty, and I won't try to explain all of it now. The majority of those explosions, if one looks at their individual features, were occurring on the ground. There is an absence of shrapnel or an absence of a significant number of casualties, if those were the air bombs. It was the air pressure which could have caused casualties within a 30-metre radius, and the witness said that there would have been 10.000 bits of shrapnel. There should have been a lot more casualties. Particularly characteristic is what happened in July when the offensive began. There -- there were no casualties at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to understand your case, and it is that so far from these bombs having been fired by the Serbs that modified air bombs, they were in fact planted by the ABiH and exploded and you -- and, to support that, you say that if there were modified air bombs you would have expected to find more shrapnel and more casualties?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at least someone who saw where the bomb came from. Only one witness was mentioned but he never appeared here before us. At least some of the people would have seen the bombs since it was daylight, but we have not heard a single witness who said that he saw a bomb flying at a relatively low speed and fall -- hit the ground. This witness says that that witness saw something and -- including the launching system mounted on a truck, and that then he saw the launching truck leave for the factory. He mentions that witness, but we haven't found a single witness in all these days who said that he saw the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But just -- we just confirm that your case is that the -- these bombs were planted by personnel of the ABiH? Isn't that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I categorically state that in most of the cases the answer is yes, absolutely so; it is my definite position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to the be clear about that. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- it misstates the evidence to stay that there were no witnesses to these air bombs in flight. I can think of one immediately, the witness who testified from -- having seen it from a -- a OP4, and I believe that there are others who have talked about the air bombs in flight. It's also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think he's saying there were no witnesses, but he said that you'd have expected to have more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. He said there were no other witnesses. He stated it quite categorically. And it's also -- it's not -- there's been no evidence that there were no witnesses to these air bombs in flight. There -- there may be not witnesses who have been identified and come to court, but that's a different thing from saying nobody saw these bombs launched or flying, which is what counsel keeps saying. Well, if nobody saw them, then how could they have been launched and fly? People -- it's our case, of course, that people did see them. It's not -- just because you haven't -- they haven't been identified and brought to court, that doesn't mean that nobody saw them. I -- I mean, it's one thing to argue but to misstate the evidence, I think, is -- is not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so as not to forget, in the case of one bomb, the Defence categorically states that it was observed to have been fired from one of the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What importance that attaches to the entire issue of air bombs, well, I wouldn't go into that right now, but at least in one case the Defence's position is that it was fired from one of the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wanted to ask the witness the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you worked on the case that had to do with the television, did you have in mind of UN report in which it is clear that people from the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at projectile that we termed an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see such a report. What I saw were two statements of military observers, if this is what you had in mind. Maybe we are talking about two different incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another five minutes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the incident of the 7th of April, in addition to everything else I have put forth. Perhaps I can show you page 102, and, in English, it is 114. So in the B/C/S, it is 102. There you state: "There are no traces of destruction from bomb fragments on the remaining walls while they should have been there, considering that the FAB-250 has a minimum of 11.000 fragments." Isn't this case -- example which shows that that bomb did not have the characteristics of a weapon which could cause catastrophic -- which would have catastrophic consequences, as is stated in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us make one thing clear, when I talk about the FAB-250, I'm talking about the one with TNT. When I talk about the -- a modified FAB-250 bomb, I'm talking about an air bomb with a fuel, fuel-air. If confirms my concept. If you look at the second photograph to the right, you will see that next to the house an air bomb exploded. On the walls you see no marks of penetration by fragments which should have been there had the bomb been filled with TNT. This is a typical example of a fuel-air bomb explosion in which the pressure of the detonation is between 20 or 30 bar, rather than several 100.000 bars. This corroborates my hypothesis that all of these projectiles were actually fuel-air projectiles. And perhaps I could add something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but I'm short of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please look at the upper picture in the right-hand side corner. It is a practical example. You see that the inner wall in the house was preserved. Only the outer walls were destroyed, whereas the inner wall remains. It is a typical characteristic of a fuel-air bomb; when the fuel migrates through or in the area it has such an impact. If there is a TNT explosion, the pressure created hits the surface, knocking it down. When we have the fuel-air, when it migrates in a -- in a space, the pressure is on both sides. Therefore, the wall remains, and this is precisely what this photograph shows, the photograph on page 102 in the upper hand -- right-hand corner. It is a very clear example of such a bomb impacting against a building. As you can see, there is not a single mark of -- any fragments. There is a wooden door in the picture, and there are no fragment marks there. The only thing that happened was the destruction of the planks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apart from the lack of fragmentation, which you say indicates it was a fuel-air bomb, would one expect to find anything else that would confirm your theory that it was a fuel-air bomb? Is there anything tangible that one would expect to find consistent with the -- a fuel-air bomb having been discharged and exploded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when a F-250 [as interpreted] air bomb explodes on the ground, depending on whether it impacts at the moment of hitting the ground or once it has penetrated the ground, it forms as crater which is between seven and 12 metres in radius, the depth of which is between 1.8 and 3.8 metres. I provided a reference about a British Army report of such effects. A crater must be there. A bomb cannot influence the surface only. In any case, it creates a crater which is at least seven and as much as 12 metres in diameter, and it uplifts enormous quantities of earth. And if we are talking about an FAB-250, it has 93 kilos of TNT. In these incidents, such effects were not present. It couldn't have happened that there were no fragments and no craters of such dimensions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, finishing up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an example of the experts conduct. In the next paragraph on the same page, perhaps I needn't read all the figures, but as for the estimated angle, it would entail mounting a launching pad at the foot of Mount Igman which would cause, or, rather, render the launching site vulnerable to infantry attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to deny that the launching site was as mentioned in the reports of the investigators? It was on page 102.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me where the investigator states that the launching site was there? Did they say it was in the village of Dolac, according to a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes but you can read it for yourself. It is on page 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we could have an English reference. I think the 102 is a B/C/S reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't it the same page, page 140, the paragraph below?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I thought there was just another reference to the village of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- to what the investigator said, I don't know, maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the English page for that other reference, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, 114.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clearly delineated the way I determined the azimuth. If we look at page 101 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you change the location at which the investigators stated the launching -- the launching pad was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can look at my methodology and the way I used to determine the direction from which the projectile came. Did you read my entire report? It is clearly stated there how I determined what the angle of impact was as well as the direction azimuth. In cases such as this one, I can only determine what the wider area was. I cannot be precise -- as precise to say it was two degrees to the right or to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude, here you state that that would imply that the launcher had to be placed right under Mount Igman, which would make it exposed to possible infantry fire. Is this why you changed the degree values and now all of a sudden you are talking about 320 degrees?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was most likely. This is the minimum position to the left where the launching site could have been in order to be able to hit that building. It doesn't preclude or exclude the previous concept. I did not rely on the witness statement, since it was the witness who mentioned the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I tried to ask you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 140 of your report in the English, and I'll tell you in a second what it is in B/C/S. It would be 125. This is in regard to the TV tower incident. Now, do you see that we -- the section entitled "investigator's opinion"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And there it says that the -- it states that the incoming direction was 280 degrees plus or ten -- plus or minus ten degrees. And then if you could look -- turn a couple of pages and follow to where your comment is. It's on page 143 of the English, where you start your comment, and, on the B/C/S, I'm not sure where it is, but I'm sure you can find it. And in the third paragraph of your comment you state that the incoming was 280 degrees. So is your -- my question is, is your opinion about the direction of fire consistent with the investigator's?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One other question. You were shown one of your prior statements, and it's in evidence now as Exhibit D170. And the President of the Trial Chamber asked you a question about this, but i just wanted to make sure it was absolutely clear because I'm not sure whether it was completely clear in the end. On page 7 in the English of that statement, and I'm afraid I don't know what it's going to be in B/C/S, but I think it's approximately the same page. It's when you're talking about the effects and use of types of bombs, in particular fuel-air bombs, and you say in the last paragraph, I think, there on the B/C/S. If we could scroll down on the B/C/S so that the bottom of the page is visible. You -- you -- you -- does that say, the beginning, technically this projectile was not perfect? Just so I'm oriented, I think ...

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And then -- and then you say in that: "Our authorities did not appreciate that these weapons are unsuited for use against military targets." Do you see that, that paragraph? Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is: Are you suggesting there in any way that the ABiH in Sarajevo had modified air bombs during the period of time that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, I have a few questions to put to you regarding some of the evidence which we have heard during this trial. And my first question relates to information that was provided to us that on some of the shrapnel pieces of some of the modified air bombs swastika signs were found, suggesting that the air bomb that had been used was a reminiscence from the Second World War. And I wonder if you could enlighten us a bit on that, and the question is: Were bombs that were left over from the Second World War used during the siege of Sarajevo, and who could have used those bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I remember it correctly, it was the Safeta Hadzica case. There was a built-up area, and, in addition to a fuel-air bomb, several mortar rounds fell, and, as for the pieces of the fuel-air bomb, it wasn't those pieces that contained the swastika, or, rather, it was the fuse of the mortar round, as far as I recall. Then a fuel-air explosive did not exist in the Second World War. It was used in Vietnam by the Americans for the first time, if this is a response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to clarify, because I thought that some of the air bombs that had been used in Sarajevo were in fact bombs that were remaining from the Second World War, and perhaps they could have been refuelled, so to say, that they could have contained TNT originally and then the TNT had been taken out and the explosive would -- would then have been replaced with air-fuel explosive. Or it could have been a smaller bomb corresponding to the FAB-100. But if your answer is that to your knowledge no bombshells remaining from the Second World War were used, except that perhaps some mortars that could have remained from the Second World War were used, then that answer satisfies my question. Is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My next question relates to the observations that apparently some of the witnesses who saw modified air bombs have offered, and I believe that at least one witness and maybe several witnesses have testified to the effects that they saw a bomb with four rockets attached to it. And my question therefore is: What sort of modified air bomb would that have been, because if I understand you correctly the FAB-100 had three rockets, while the FAB-250 had only one big rocket attached to it. So if an air bomb was observed with four rockets, then what sort of bomb would that have been?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is the Russian air bomb, Potok 500 with four rocket boosters. The code-name is KREMA-4. In the area of Sarajevo, the FAB-250 with three rocket boosters were used. On occasion, and there is documents to support it by the RS army, that sometimes they used bombs with two rocket boosters. There are orders in existence as to that. When reading investigator reports, I noticed that rocket boosters of 120-millimetre GRAD were used, these are of Russian make. It has two pipes connecting the boosters, and once such a bomb impacts, even four or five cylinders could be found on occasion, and with laypeople this was -- create an impression that there were more than three rocket boosters. This is what I came across when reading such reports, but each time it said 122-millimetres deep, and -- sorry, the pieces were 120 by 700 millimetres. And the length of a rocket booster is about 1800 millimetres. That would be my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now my next question relates to observations offered by other witnesses regarding the sound. It has been extensively covered in your report, I am fully aware of that, but somehow the information that I have read in your report does not quite match the witnesses' observations. You see, we have had witnesses who said that they saw a bomb coming flying slowly over the sky and making the sound as -- making a sound that reminded them of a jet plane. What I do not understand and what I'm asking you to explain to me, if you can, is: If I understood you correctly the engine only burns for a couple of seconds, two or three or maybe four seconds, and then the rocket has exhausted its sources of propelling. And from that moment on, the -- the bomb just continues ballistically. If a witness then observes the bomb coming flying over the sky and hearing a sound that is very distinct, what sound would that have been? Would that have been while the engine -- while the rocket engine was still burning or is there a sound even after the rocket has exhausted its fuel? What I'm asking, I guess, is that the sound of a mortar is very distinct. It has a whistling sound when it lands. And my question is therefore: Would a modified air bomb have a similar sound, even after the rocket has exhausted its fuel? Or would it be silent?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you put the question exceptionally well. There two segments, one is the launching segment with a high-pitch sound, and it is quite loud when the rocket engines are working. It lasts for about two seconds. That is one phase. If you go to page 60, you will see that the stabilisers or the tail-fins are rather small in terms of their -- in terms of their area, and they are supposed to direct the rocket once it leaves the launch pad. What this means is that watching laterally, people can hear a humming sound, like a cylinder aeroplane engine, the engine of a small plane flying over an area, but this is only laterally. If you stand in front of the projectile, it flies at a designated speed and can you hear it. It is a typical sound of rotation. It is a hissing sound of air going through the pieces of rocket, the streaming of air, and it goes for both the FAB-250 and for the other one. They both have tail-fins which rotate the rocket, and it is stated at page 68 and 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't have the B/C/S; unfortunately, I only have the English. But I'll find that information, but thank you very much. So just to confirm: A witness who could hear a modified air bomb, a witness could hear a modified air bomb even after the engine had exhausted its fuel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You hear the sound for as long as the projectile is flying ballistically as of the moment when the rocket engine stopped working and the moment of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question, and I have just a few more questions left. My next question is the observation that we have been offered by expert by -- sorry, by police officers, investigators and by UNMOs, namely the fact that both for mortars and apparently for modified air bombs the tail-fin for a mortar and the rockets for a modified air bomb remain in the crater once the device has exploded. And -- and I wonder if you can provide us just with some sort of information about how come that the tail-fin remains in the crater. One would have thought that it would be blasted away from the point of explosion. What is the dynamic process of the tail-fin remaining in the crater or, as we see on page -- I just found it a while ago. I think on page 119 in the English version, we see on the upper-right corner a crater with -- with the remainders of the rockets? Why are these remnants not blown away?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I will try to explain about mortars, if you agree, and then we can go back to this specific case. In the case of a mortar, if I may use this photograph to explain this in detail, when a mortar hits the ground, when it flies at a certain velocity and impacts against a target and explodes, and this part is thrown off at a velocity of about 180 metres per second. This is in the case of a 120-millimetre mortar. If the incoming velocity and the velocity of the bit being thrown off is the same, and that is about 170 metres per second, we are likely to find the stabiliser or the tail-fin. And this was the case with Markale 2. When the velocity of a missile, when impacting is less than the velocity of the bits being thrown off, this will bounce about 50 or 100 metres and will no longer be at the same place where the explosion took place. When the velocity is greater than 170 metres per second, this piece will continue to fly and will drill its way into the ground. But I'm only talking about 120-millimetre mortars. With 80-millimetre and 60-millimetre mortar, it will be very difficult to find a stabiliser or a tail-fin anywhere near the site of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: All the answer was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, Did you understand that your last answer was translated into French. So I kindly ask you to repeat it. And can I -- when you repeat your answer, could you then include one piece of information, namely, the question -- answer to the question of whether the tail-fin is separated from the shell while the mortar is still descending. Because I thought that -- that the tail-fin would remain on the shell until the moment of explosion. So -- so could you include in your answer also answer to the question whether the tail-fin is separated from the shell -- from the case itself before the mortar explodes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortar has a body and the bearer of the tail-fin and they are together until the mortar hits the ground. When there is an explosion, the body splinters into thousands of pieces and they fly at a velocity of several thousand metres per second. This body is massive. It's about four and a half kilos. It can't possibly splinter and there are three possible things that can possibly happen depending on the incoming velocity. When the incoming velocity is about the same, which is about 180 metres per second, in those cases we shall find the stabiliser near the place where the explosion occurred. If the velocity is lower than that, which usual happens when the range is low, then you -- one doesn't find the body of the projectile nearby. It's usually at a distance of about 150 or 200 metres from the explosion itself, depending on the angle and the velocity. The third case is the case of Markale 3. The projectile flies at a high velocity than 180 metres per second, and then the stabiliser pad continues to fly and drills its way into the ground. Then -- it was then we found it, but this is only possible with 120-millimetre mortars. With these rocket systems, for example, if there was some TNT in the warhead, the same thing would have happened. These rocket boosters would have been bounced out of the crater because the velocity is about 150 to 200 metres per second at the point of impact. And taking into account that fact that if you have an air bomb, FAB-250, and it contains about 93 kilograms of explosives, it -- it would have been bounced off about 100 metres and so would the stabilisers have been. I did not want to use that as an argument because the primary thing for me was no shrapnel, and that is the key to the situation. If an air bomb lands next to a building at a 10-metre distance, there is a white wall, and the white wall shows absolutely no shrapnel at all, then the situation is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be reminded to slow down drastically, otherwise we are absolutely unable to follow what he is saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast, too quickly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Zecevic, relates to some of the considerations that might have been made at the Pretis factory when these bombs were developed. And when I put my question to you, I remind you that you are still under oath, and that are you not accused in this case. My question is whether, to your knowledge, the possibility of using these newly developed modified air bombs on civilian targets was ever discussed at Pretis, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you mean up to 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Up to 1992 and until 1995, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the factory on the 17th of April, 1992, and I was no longer able to even access the factory. Up until that point in time there had been only been one option, to develop a fuel-air bomb which was meant to be used to target tank convoys and certainly not to target civilians, or civilian settlements. At the same time there was a plan to develop a fuel-air grenade that was supposed to be laid in places where tanks were expected. Throughout my time with the JNA, it was never part of its doctrine, not even in the remotest possible way, to use any weapon at all against civilians. At least that was the case while we were still in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But yet you say that the precision-ness of these weapons were extremely poor. So one would have thought that if you were developing a new technique of launching these air bombs by using rockets and you knew that it was very difficult to target with any degree of precision, then how could one have avoided discussing the possibilities that they would be falling on civilian areas and therefore one would have thought that, in developing these weapons, extreme cautions were to be -- or would have to be taken when using them, that is to say that -- that the bombs could then only be used against tanks, as you said, in an open field where there was no risk of the bomb dropping down in the civilian area. Were these considerations made in your time?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to emphasise this. Back in 1991, for example, the Pretis factory sent to Iraq, for example, about 700 missiles with a range of 50 kilometres and these were developed specifically for Iraq. These missiles were the so-called Orkan missiles, but they were not part of the JNA armoury because they didn't meet the standards that existed at the time. I'm talking about up to 1992. The destructive potential, the accuracy, and the effectiveness that was called for at the time. In August 1992 when armed conflicts erupted in Yugoslavia, the rockets were transferred to the Novi Sad Corps. I'm telling you about the general idea. Yugoslavia was pumping a lot of money into developing its rocket systems, but the standards were very high. Ammunition had to be reliable. One had to know where a missile would end up, and what the impact deviation would be. Based on that, you could assess what the targets would have been. However, the course that the war took and the respective powers of the parties involved caused a disbalance to the morality of warfare in Yugoslavia. Up until 1992, not a single rocket artillery or mortar system could have been part of the armoury that had not been long in developing, sometimes between five - possibly seven - and ten years. No single system was ever used. Never was a decision taken to use a system that had not been developed for longer than a year. That was a rule. There is an -- actually book of rules adopted by the supreme staff the JNA describing the evolutionary progress of each and every weapon, all tests that had to be run, and there had to be independent committees assessing certain weapons and whether it met certain technical standards or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that normal screening process then, according to what you're saying, was not observed when it came to the use of -- of the FABs-100 and FABs-250.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have an answer on the 92 ter motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree. We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be handled by Mr. Sachdeva. It's Mr. Higgs, another expert witness. And I've lost track of when the break is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We did break early, but I think we'll just go to -- to 20 past.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The reality is that with the -- with the change that's going to occur, we're going to use -- we're going to have basically the time for him to sit down and say hello. So might -- maybe it would be more efficient if we'd -- if you'd -- if Your Honours don't mind. We're happy to do it any way you like, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll just take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And Mr. Sachdeva you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you start by stating your full name and your place and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: My name is Richard James Higgs. My date of birth is the 20th of the 10th, 1959, and my place of birth is Nottingham in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, did you prepare expert reports, three expert reports for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did those reports pertain to an incident at the marketplace on the 28th of August, 1995, an incident at Livanjska Street on the 8th of November, 1994, at 1525 and 1725 hours and, lastly, related to an incident on the 18th of June, 1995, at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I start I would like the registrar assign Exhibit numbers to the reports. I can read out the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The first report related to the firing incident at the marketplace is 03119; the second is 03120; and the third, that is the supplement to the expert report, is 03121.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these will become Prosecution Exhibit P588 through P590 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, for your benefit and also for the benefit of the Court I'm just going to explain the sequence of my examination. I will first ask you questions about your background and expertise. I will then move on to general information about mortars, how they are fired, their accuracy, and their range. We will then discuss crater analysis, and at the last section I will move on to the specific incidents that you have written your reports on. Let me start by asking you were you in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I served in the -- for 22 years' service in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did you do for the British Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I served with the Royal Artillery and with the Small Arms School Corps, and within the Small Arms School Corps I was the division instructor which is the senior-most technical mortar position within the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you work for the Small Arms School Corps, when did you start your work there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I started working with them in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the army, did you have a rank and, if you did, what was that rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. My rank within the army was called quartermaster sergeant instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was your rank, that is the quartermaster sergeant instructor, was that determinative of the -- the work you did related to mortars and the technical aspects of mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The rank did not bear any resemblance to my appointment as senior mortar officer. I worked on an appointment far higher than my rank as I supported the British government and the British Army at very senior levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can I ask you this then: When you say you were the senior-most technical mortar position instructor in the British Army, when it came to questions arising out of the use of mortars and the technical factors related to mortars, did the - how should I say it? - did the buck stop with you? Were you the senior-most person in the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was the senior advisor so any rulings or instructions that I gave had to be acted upon. Regardless if a senior officer wanted to do otherwise, my appointment was such that they would carry out my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in your career related to the army and to mortars, did you undertake mortar investigations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have undertaken many mortar investigations for the British Army, for various foreign armies, and also in the past for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it your investigations were not just conducted in the UK but other places in the world; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what types of investigations did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have undertaken investigations where there has been loss of life during training, criminal investigations where I have had to identify what has happened and why, and also undertaken investigations where it's been important to find out type of weapons used, directions of fire, possible intentions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually that -- your answer led into my next question, which was: When you conduct a mortar investigation, what are you attempting to establish?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I need to establish the type of mortar used, the direction of fire, and the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you also presumably -- all these factors, would they assist you in determining the likely firing point and therefore the people that fired the rounds?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From this information, that then gives me the information where I can then, using my experience, come to conclusions where the fire came from and the likely intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your investigations, did you conduct what is called crater analyses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, these are an integral part of the most of the investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just very generally, we're going get into detail later, but when you undertake a crater analysis, what are you looking for specifically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: With the crater, it forms a pattern so I can use that pattern in my determination. I'm also looking for probably parts off the projectile to assist me in my investigation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the pattern that you look at, what does that assist you in concluding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The mortar gives a very definite and distinctive pattern on the ground. That pattern can be used to determine the bearing or direction of fire, and can also be used to indicate the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right. And we'll get to those aspects later. So let me ask you this: In your career, how many mortar investigations, roughly, have you undertaken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Probably in excess of a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, at the moment you not with the British Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct. I retired from the British Army a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you -- although you've retired, do you interact with the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Although retired, the individuals who are now doing what I used to do still occasionally phone me up for advice, suggestions, because of my experience that I spent in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you are almost sort of an unofficial consultant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, have you testified here at the ICTY before coming here today.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. I presented evidence on the Galic case where I look at various incidents of mortars engaging civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just before I ask you more questions about that, in preparing your expert reports for the Galic case, did you have the occasion to visit Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, prior and for part of that report I spent a number of days in that area, both within the city and driving around all the surrounding areas, looking at the confrontation lines, as they were, all the major parts of the city, to get a feel for the whole topological layout and the position, and basically what both sides would have seen at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long were you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I think the visit was four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask you this now, just in relation to Sarajevo, how conclusive of a place or city is it to the deployment of mortar batteries, mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: For a mortar commander who would be looking at -- or if he'd be attacking Sarajevo, it is an ideal position, because the city sits below high ground, which surrounds it, which is ideal for any type of mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say "ideal," just very briefly explain, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Well, because a mortar is technically an indirect fire weapon, you need to be able to, of course, see the target, ideally at as long a range as possible. Because of the layout of the land in that area, it is possible to place mortars on higher ground overlooking the target at a distance far enough away so they are safe themselves but still to have direct line of sight to the target, which is a big issue in increasing accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If a mortar battery commander did not have direct line of sight, how would they go about identifying targets? How is that typically done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When they can obtain to -- a direct line of sight, the mortar is normally fired using an observer in the same way as artillery is used for long distances. The observer will then direct the fire on to the target. This can be done with mortars as well. But mortars can also fire what is known as direct fire, if they have direct line of sight, which then takes out any errors as an observer may have had, and is a far more accurate way of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And, as I said, I'll ask you more detailed questions about that. I just want to get back for a moment to your evidence, your reports regarding the Galic case. You said that you conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think it might be of interest if you could just put the question to the witness whether he knew that observers were actually used during this, the conflict in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I will just repeat the question from His Honour Judge Harhoff. Do you have any knowledge as to whether observers were deployed in the conflict in the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have no direct evidence they were, but some of the mortar locations that were sighted around the town were in such positions where they could not directly see into the town, so those ones must have had some form of observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Does that clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, just before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that there had to be observers but that's if the target -- if the shots were aimed at a specific target, otherwise there is no need for an observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were just going to fire anywhere, and did not care where the round went, then, yes, you are correct. You don't need an observer. But if you want the round to go accurately on to a target, then you would either need to see it directly yourself or use an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, before this -- this slight deviation I was asking you about the Galic case and your investigation into incidents there. You said that they concerned incidents where civilian casualties were incurred. Just very briefly, what was the subject matter of your investigations, your expert reports into -- into these incidents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In all the cases we were trying to determine, of course, the calibre of the weapon that was fired, the direction it came from, angle of descent in each case, and then from that to determine the likely firing positions and possible intentions from the type of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall which incidents that you -- you worked on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: One of the major cases I worked on was the Markale market incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in those -- in those incidents did, as you aid that you -- that was a subject matter of your evidence, did you come to any conclusions as to the likely firing position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In the -- those cases, it was determined that because of the types of -- from the crater analysis that we carried that the fire had come from across the confrontation lines originating from different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say across the confrontation lines, which party to the conflict controlled the area where you concluded was the likely firing position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When I say beyond the confrontation line that would then be into the Serb-held territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on to the general sort of functioning of mortars. Firstly, why don't you start by telling the Court what type of mortars are there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There are basically types and they are grouped by their calibre. You have light, medium, and heavy mortars. Mortars of around 85-millimetre calibre are classed as medium mortars, and then those of 120-millimetre calibre and bigger are classed as heavy mortars. So those are the main categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And very briefly, how -- how is a mortar typically fired whether it be 82-millimetre or 120-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The majority are muzzle loaded, which means that you drop the round down the barrel. You can get some breech-loaded mortars of the larger calibre but these are not as common as the muzzle-loaded version. So the round is dropped down the barrel, it strikes a firing pin at the base of the barrel which then causes the round, of course, then to ignite, and then the charge push it back up the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you mention charge, and again I'm going to -- well, I'll leave that and follow my sequence but I just -- I'll come back to the definition of charge and what a charge is. But at this point I would like you to tell the Court, what are mortars designed for? Typically what are they designed to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: A mortar round is designed primarily to kill personnel. They are not destruct weapon, i.e., for blowing up large targets, buildings and so on. They are primarily used to kill personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from the design, how would that be achieved.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The mortar bomb, because it has a slower and normally steeper trajectory than, let's say, artillery, which means that the round tends to explode at ground level, first of all, does not tend to dig in as far as artillery rounds. Also, the rounds are made to fragmentate, i.e., burst into smaller -- far smaller pieces than artillery ammunition, which is why they are more effective against what we call soft skin or personnel-type targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is there anything you can say about the angle at which mortars --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Because of their angle, they tend to come in steeper than most other direct-fire weapons. It mean that most of the blast is then directed at floor level and you do not waste blast into the ground like with some shells, so you get maximum effect from each round.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with respect to range, firstly with an 82-millimetre, what is the maximum range?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Mortars obviously differ slightly depending on the type of ammunition, but the 82-millimetre, which was used a lot in this case, is around four and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The 120's, again very slightly, but they could give you a maximum range of up between seven or eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How does one increase or decrease the range of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Most muzzle-loading mortars have a set of charges which go around the tail section of the round. These are called augmenting cartridges, or some people call them cheeses. They slide over the tail section of the round. The more you slide over, increases the charge. The more you have on the tail section, the longer the range you will achieve from that mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so with a 120-millimetre mortar, if you know, what -- how many charges can one put on a 120-millimetre metre, at least with the ones that were deployed in the former Yugoslavia, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Most of the rounds used here were using charge systems up to six. So that would be six different charges on the tail sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it from your previous answer, charge six would give you the highest possible range, highest possible distance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Again, with respect to range, how significant is elevation in that calculation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Well, a mortar can effect its range in two ways, either by changing the charge or by changing the elevation or a combination of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to move on to accuracy. Firstly, generally, how accurate are mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The modern mortar, and when I say "modern," we're talking now mortars in the last 30, 40 years, are very accurate weapon systems. They are not to -- the area weapon as of probably used in the two main world wars. They are now very accurate weapon systems indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could take to you page 3 of your initial report, and that is the report related to the Markale incident, and I think it's also page 3 in the B/C/S version, I take it you have the reports there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On page 3 you talk about the factors that determine accuracy. And I want to ask you a few questions about a few of these factors. If you go down the list you will see that you have mentioned--

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fail to understand. Which Markale incident are we talking about? The 5th of February, 1995, or the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm talking about the 28th of August, 1995. The witness has not produced a report for the first Markale incident for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you see that list of factors that you have there, and I want to ask you about what you've indicated here called the stability of the base plate. Can you just briefly explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Well, mortars are a mobile weapons system, and before they fire with any accuracy, they have to be stable in the ground. They have a form of a plate which they sit on which has to be located firmly in the ground before they can achieve any accuracy. This can be down by firing normally to get this plate, which is known as "to bed in," solidly into the ground. Without this, you cannot achieve the highest accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your opinion, if mortars have been positioned in a location over a long period of time, would that increase or decrease the stability of the base plate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It would be a major advantage to the stability of the weapon, because you have been able to leave it in place for so long to have a really stable platform to fire from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I know that you've already answered it, but just to be clear, how does that affect the accuracy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Because when the weapon fires, it is no longer sinking into the ground, which then affects the accuracy on range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And maybe I will just ask you this: Given your work for this case as also for the Galic case, do you have an opinion as to whether the mortar batteries were indeed positioned for a long period of time in the same place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It seems from -- after when I did my visit and from the positions that the mortars tended to be in positions for some time so they could achieve this higher stability.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sticking with this list regarding accuracy, I want to -- again, you've -- you've started to explain when you talk about the skill of the mortar observer, but just for the sake of completeness, can you explain that factor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: If the mortar is being used for indirect fire, obviously the skill of the observer is crucial to get the highest accuracy on to the target, because his orders to the mortar will affect, of course, where they fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And lastly, you've indicated here the prior recording of targets. Again, please briefly explain what you mean by that and how that affects the accuracy of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: If it's possible with a mortar to increase accuracy, you want to record targets or reference points in the area you're firing into. Because this being a town, it's got a lot of natural reference points anyway, like church spires, main buildings, and so on, but also every time you fire you would record the firing data to certain parts of that area. And the longer you're there and the more you fire, the more reference points you can obtain, and the more you have, the higher the accuracy rate of you then engaging in where the target would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in an urban environment like Sarajevo where the conflict is carried on for some time, do you have an opinion as to whether targets would have been prerecorded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I think most definitely because the area lends itself to that and it would speed up engagement time it would make engagements more accurate, and it would save wasting ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you again to sort of characterise the accuracy. You've mentioned that the accuracy rate would be higher, are we talking about a target that could be engaged in one shot? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to command issues. You have already mentioned that the 120-millimetre mortar and the 82-millimetre mortars are described as heavy and medium weaponry respectively. In your upon opinion, how valuable an asset are these mortars for the military command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Any indirect-fire weapon system is a huge asset to a commander because of the types ammunition they can fire. That is why these tend to be controlled very closely on their use, because of course you do not wish to waste such a valuable asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So typically, how would the deployment and launching of mortars be -- be controlled? By which level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Medium and heavy mortars are controlled at command level again to prevent some, if you like, lower rank local commander from just firing at something and wasting such a valuable asset. They tend to be commanded at the more senior command level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So do you have an opinion in respect to this case whether these mortars would have been commanded by -- by senior commandered or even indeed the commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It seems very unlikely they would have been allowed just to fire on their own. In my opinion, they would have come under the most senior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I now want to move on to -- to look into detail about crater analysis. You have -- you have answered this, but when you conduct a crater analysis, I understand that you said you're looking for the type of round, the direction of fire, and the angle of descent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: Are these factors important for the determination as to the likely firing position of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's start with direction of fire. Again, you've explained it briefly, but I'm going to ask you to use a photograph to go into a little bit more detail as to how this is determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could move to -- it's page 3 of your supplemental report, and Mr. President, Your Honours, that is 65 ter 03121. For the benefit of the Defence, I also think it's page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you have that report with you, Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on page 3 you'll see these two photographs. And for your answer, I just want you to ignore the measurements that we see here. But just explain how you would determine the angle -- sorry, the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: You can see from the pictures you have the first crater in the centre, which is where the rounds exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I just stop you there for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think for the benefit of the Court it might be useful if you are able to -- is the witness able to mark this still and for it to be saved as an additional exhibit. It seems that this is fine. If the court usher could hand -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, can I ask you, is it easier for you to work off the top or the bottom photograph for this explanation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Probably easier to work off the top one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. So on the top one, you started to talk about the first crater in the centre. Can you just mark that position with the figure 1, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: You mean the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It would be -- that's the position of the dot that I put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you could just place the figure 1. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And before I interrupted you, you started by saying you have the first crater in the centre. If you could please carry on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, the first crater at the point of impact is the one, and I'll show -- mark the extremities of that just to make it clear. Which is that one there, and I'll just call that number 2. That shows the initial crater at the -- at the point of impact. But just above that, you can see marks in the tarmac that has been caused by the shrapnel, which is what we call the second crown. Those marks are these here -- I'll just put an arrow to them, and you can see they go around in a fan shape. This second crown will always be facing towards the direction of fire. And the second crown and its position on the ground and the general pattern we can then use for calculating the bearing or the direction of fire, and from the overall pattern we can also determine the approximate angle of descent because the pattern -- the general pattern on the ground will change as the angle of descent changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll move on to the angle of descent in a moment. But just for now, could you put the figure 3 by the arrow that you've indicated there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so just to conclude your answer, is it fair to say that where one sees the preponderance of the -- of the marks on the ground in a crater, that would indicate the direction from which the projectile came. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this into evidence, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, on the photograph I see that you placed a line at the second crown, at the level of the second crown. According to you, the -- the distance between the centre of the crater to that second crown, is that useful to determine the origin of fire; and, if so, what would happened if there were two projectiles shot from the same mortar, one falling on a hard surface, like tarmac, and the other one falling on a soft surface, like -- like mud. I guess that the distance between the core and the second crown will be different, depending on the terrain that the projectile landed on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer your first question, yes, the distance from point of impact to the centre of the second crown is a measurement we do use in ballistic calculation. Craters that you get on soft ground still produce this general pattern. However, on soft ground, grass, for instance, it is far more difficult to measure accurately because the pattern does not stand out as well as it does on hard ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to inform His Honour Judge Mindua, the ballistic calculations that the witness has just spoken about, I'm going to lead into that in -- in about a minute so that should -- that should hopefully become clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And for the -- for the next exercise with respect to the angle of descent, can I still have the page on the screen, please. Mr. Higgs, from that page, if we -- sticking with that page, firstly, which photograph is better suited for you to explain how one -- well, let me start by asking you this, a more general question. I'm sorry. How does one normally determine the angle of descent from a crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Angle of descent can be calculated in two ways. The first way, ideally, would be using what is called a fuse furrow. If you don't have a fuse furrow then what I have to use, ballistic calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is that fuse furrow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: A fuse furrow is a hole in the ground cause by the fuse around -- when it explodes, it's then driven into the ground and produces like a long small hole into the ground, and then from that it is possible to place a measuring stick into the hole and then record the angle of descent from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When is a fuse furrow typically created?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: You tend to get fuse furrows on the softer ground. Grass, that sort of thing, you'll get good fuse furrows. The harder the ground, the less chance you're going to get one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So is one less likely to see a fuse furrow on, for example, a road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: A main road is probably one of the hardest substances that a mortar will be fired at, and normally you would not get a fuse furrow when it is fired on to this type of surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that a fuse furrow produces a long small hole. Can you just give an idea to the Court as to the dimensions of this long hole?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Fuse furrows can differ slightly in there their dimensions but normally a hole will be a couple of centimetres wide and probably anything up to 30 or even 40, 50 centimetres long on soft ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And let me just ask you this: Can a fuse furrow be used to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In methodologies used for determination of direction, the use of a fuse furrow should not be used because they are not an accurate means of determining direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. So you mentioned the fuse furrow and you said there were two methods to determine the angle of descent. What is the other method.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The other method is ballistic calculation, when you don't have no fuse furrow to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And to explain this ballistic calculation, which photograph would be best suited for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Probably the picture at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. If we could look at the bottom photograph, perhaps enlarge it, thank you. And again, if you want to take a pen and explain the measurements that are taken.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The first measurement that you need is the measurement across the initial crater. That will be the measurement from the front to the back of the crater, so from the line there to the rear of the crater. That is the first calculation that we need. Having done that calculation, what we would then look for is a measurement marked on this photograph as measurement L. Because -- that one there on the picture. What we then look at is the type of round that had been fired, because we use the dimensions of the round. We have to look from -- the measurement from the tip of the round to the centre of the body of the round. So that is the -- the other calculation. What we then do is -- the calculation where we look at the dimension from the tip of the round to the centre of the body, and then by using cosines and dividing in the length between point of impact and the centre of the second crown here, we can then come up with an angle of descent. So the measurement, L, which is marked there on the screen is a crucial measurement that we require.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In that measurement, L, the top of the line, is that the second crown?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The second crown, as we call it, is marked in the centre of the area where the shrapnel has cut out the indentations, so it's marked to the centre. That's what is called the second crown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this still into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I want to ask you about -- well, let me ask you this: What is a tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The tail-fin is the construction at the base of the round which has small fins that protrude from it which, when the bomb is in flight, it gives it stability, and the tail-fin also gives you a means by which you can attach your augmenting cartridges, i.e., the charges to the round.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can a tail-fin be used to assist in a mortar investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The tail-fins can you used in two ways. First of all, if you have a tail-fin, it tends to be the only large part usually of the mortar bomb that is left after it's exploded, and the tail-fins will normally have the ammunition batch numbers stamped on them. So it will help you identify the calibre and the type of ammunition straight away. But they can also be of some use when they are still lodged in the mortar crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When would you typically find a tail-fin lodged into a crater? What circumstances would allow for that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The tail-fin do not always lodge into the craters because of different circumstances like the hardness of the ground and also the velocity in which the round struck the ground, and this will be dependant upon the charge that the mortar has been fired at. There is normally a higher percentage of tail-fins in craters when the rounds have been fired on the higher charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "higher charge," you mean fired from the longer distance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. The charges which would give the mortars the longer ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you did mention circumstances like the hardness of the ground. In other words, one could have a mortar that was fired from a farther distance but if it landed on hard ground, that you may not see the tail-fin stuck in the crater. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the specific incidents that you worked on. And let me start by asking you this: At least in relation to the Markale incident and the Livanjska Street incident at 1525 hours and the Livanjska Street incident that is the first shell at 1730 hours. In your opinion, were there good quality craters produced from those incidents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They've all produced good patterns from the shrapnel on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were they able to assist you in your conclusions and investigations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. Those patterns were sufficient to be able to confirm bearings, and from that obviously they've been able to assist me in my investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's move to the Markale incident. Now, can you confirm that you -- you reviewed photographs from this incident and a video taken after the explosion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were those photographs and the video, were they of sufficient quality for you to again come to conclusions, accurate conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also -- if you can confirm to the Court, did you review the Bosnian police report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The French UN report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The initial UNMO UN investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And finally the UNPROFOR G2 investigation, G2 report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sticking to the Bosnian police report and actually, in general, and please take your knowledge and experience that you used in the Galic case, but in general what can you say about the competence and the correctness of the methodology employed by the Bosnian police investigators when they conducted crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From all the investigations and reports I have seen of theirs, they use correct methodologies and are very competent at crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With the Markale incident, were you able to come to a conclusion as to the -- the direction of fire of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, by using the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from your review of the reports -- well, let me ask you this, the G2 report, the fourth investigation, do you recall what their conclusion was as to the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They disagreed with all the other reports and came up with a direction -- I think between 220 and 240 degrees, which was completely different from all the other reports which gave a direction nearer 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The G2 report that came to a determination of 220, 240 degrees, do you recall what that was based upon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The concern I had for that report was that they took that direction from, as they called it, the fuse furrow, which, as I've said before, is not an accepted way of calculating bearing, and none of the other investigating teams who produced reports of that incident even reported a fuse furrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
