utterances.text: In your opinion, and in your experience, if there had indeed been a fuse furrow, would the three prior investigations -- would investigators overlooked this if there was one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They would not have overlooked it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you -- well, let me ask you this. Do you recall where the mortar projectile exploded in this incident? Was it on the pavement or was it on the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This particular round exploded on a road, obviously between two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you earlier testified that on a road one is less likely to see a fuse furrow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so what is your conclusion as to the direction of fire? Is it closer to 220/240 or is it closer to 170?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Using the photographs, I was able to determine the direction from the pattern, first of all, the way in which the round landed on the road. I then related that to the direction that the road actually ran along. And I was able then to plot that and the direction comes out closer to 170 degrees and that it does to 220/240 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm now going to actually ask you to use that photograph to explain to the Court exactly how you came to that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could move to the -- if I could ask for the first report to be brought up, that is 65 ter 03119, and if we can move to page 12 in the English, and I understand that it is page 12 in the B/C/S, or perhaps page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I'm going to ask you hopefully pointed questions so you can explain. You see a measurement there on the photograph. Well, firstly, is that -- let me ask you, is that the crater at the Markale marketplace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You see a measurement that -- you see a line where you have indicated 275 degrees.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When you look at the street map of Sarajevo, the road that this impact landed on runs along an approximate direction of 275 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 185 degrees, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It just shows the right angle to 275 obviously a 90-degree angle to that one, the 185 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then using those measurements you came up with the 175.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing I did was look at the pattern, where you can see the crater in the centre and of course the shrapnel marks coming away from it to identify which way the crater was facing, first of all, and it's facing towards the building, towards the direction of the bicycles you can see on the photograph. Then by calculating of course which way the road runs on the map, I could come up with that bearing, and then relating the thicker lines through the centre of the pattern of the crater it comes up with a direction of approximately 175 degrees, as it's marked there on the picture. You can also see that from that picture, the dotted line, as if the crater had landed in that road at 220 degrees, that shows the direction that the crater should be facing, and you can clearly see from the pattern of the crater that it does not face that way at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with the 220 degrees, if indeed it had come at 220 degrees, would that affect the direction in which the road was going in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: If on this road the round had come in at 220 degrees, the pattern would be -- when that picture turned to the right quite a lot. On this particular road along that direction, that pattern faces nowhere near 220 degrees and I say faces closer to 170, 180 degrees, that sort of figure .

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I know that you've explained this, the direction of the projectile, but just to resolve any possible confusion, you have an arrow where you have indicated 175. You have an arrow going towards the bicycles. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you just take a pen and indicate the arrow from which the direction -- from which the projectile came from, in the direction from which the projectile came from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender that still into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, in addition to the direction of fire, did you come to any conclusions as to the angle of descent? And if you did, what were they, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: On the angle of descent, because of the lack of reported fuse furrow by the first three investigations, I looked at the ballistic calculations the Bosnian authorities had used to calculate. The first calculation they'd used was 67 degrees to clear the building. That was the minimum it must have been just to get over the building in front. From their calculations, they came up with an angle of descent nearer to 70 degrees by using, as I say, the crater analysis and their dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is there anything about the pattern of the crater that in your opinion enables you to confirm or support that conclusion that it was 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. If you remember the first picture of the crater that we looked at a few minutes ago, there was a definite first crater, then there was a gap before we come to our second crown and the second row of shrapnel marks. We have no marks on the other side of the impact crater. When an angle of descent starts to get steeper, the pattern changes because you now start to get shrapnel marks on both sides of the crater, which is what you have got in this case here, which would indicate that it has come in as a higher angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In addition to the direction of fire, the angle of descent, were you able to establish the type of round?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The type of round identified again by the investigating bodies, because of the pieces left at the scene, they recovered the tail-fins and small pieces of the fuse, and it was from that they could identify that this bomb was 120 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from their investigation and their conclusions as to the direction of fire and the angle of descent, do you have any reason to question or disagree with the finding, that it was a 120-millimetre round?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have got no reason to disagree with those first three reports. As I said, their findings, their methodology, their calculations, everything were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier on in evidence that the determination of the type of round, the angle of descent, and the direction of fire assists or are important in determining the likely firing position. With respect to this incident, did you come to a conclusion as to the likely firing position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the angle of descent calculated, then by using range tables which are a ballistic table that show you all the ranges that can be achieved at different charges and all elevations, it was possible to plot back to the most likely firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there for one second. You said "range tables." Were these range tables, did they relate to mortars that were used in the JNA or other types of mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They were mortars relating to the JNA specific to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And perhaps we could move to page 13 and 14 on this report and I'll ask you questions about the possible firing position. If you just go to the next page, page 13 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- Mr. Higgs, you will see that you have -- under the section entitled summary, you have the possible firing positions. You see you have indicated 900 metres on charge 1, 1.600 metres on charge 2, 2.400 metres on charge 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the umpteenth time today, I don't have the page reference for the B/C/S, nor do I have that type of information on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why not? You should have it on the screen. What's the page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's page 13 of the English, and it's the next page of the page that we were looking at beforehand, so I presume it just follows on from where Mr. Tapuskovic was in the B/C/S version. It's up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it should be on his screen now. It's on your screen now, Mr. Tapuskovic. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm there is no image. That's the first thing. It's not the same thing at all. This is the second or the third time. I didn't mean to make an issue out of this, but I simply don't have it in B/C/S and that continues to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you don't have the picture on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I ask why that is. I don't know who can answer that. The court deputy or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I perhaps can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can answer it, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Or at least I can attempt to. What's happened here is when the reports in the English language are translated, the text is translated without the maps and the pictures. In other words, the maps and the pictures can be referred to in the English version. Because the maps contain arrows, pictures could contain figures which can, in my submission, be readily accessed in the English version. Of course the text doesn't appear to have the maps when they are translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the picture or the text that you wish to focus on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I had related first to the text where the charges are indicated, and I'm now going to move on to a map which is on the following page, and the map that is indicated in the English version is -- in my submission, does not require translation. In fact, it's a map from the ABiH which has markings in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any picture at all. If I had the picture, or a photograph perhaps, I'd be quite happy in fact. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a photograph now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. I have it now. But it's with the English original. Never mind, I'll just try to follow. It's not that important, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think your assessment of the import appears to different from Mr. Sachdeva's. But continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to -- this section is going to take roughly ten minutes, and I see we are very close to the adjournment time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we adjourn. Very well. We will take the adjournment until tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of April, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
